\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Large language models now write fluently in many languages, but almost everything known about telling their outputs apart comes from English, and the cost of an interpretable representation against character $n$-grams has not been measured on content-controlled multilingual data. We collected \NCollected{} persuasive essays from five frontier large language models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.7, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4 Pro) in seven languages from \NPrompts{} content-matched prompts, described each text by \NFeatures{} features computed the same way on Universal Dependencies parses in every language, and scored five-way authorship attribution with leave-one-prompt-out cross-validation. Logistic regression reaches \LRmin{}--\LRmax{} accuracy in every language (chance \Chance{}). Across a coarse pre-registered resource ranking we detect no decline (\Beta{} log-odds per rank step, 95\% CI \BetaLo{} to \BetaHi{}), an interval that admits a drop of up to \SteepestDeclinePts{} points. Character $n$-grams are \GapNGmin{}--\GapNGmax{} points more accurate within a language (Holm-significant in \NGsigN{} of seven); given the same unlabelled adaptation to the target language, the features transfer between languages at mean \TransferOff{} against \NGFairOff{} for $n$-grams. In each language, five features chosen on the training folds reach \CurveKfiveShareMin{}--\CurveKfiveShareMax{}\% of the full set's macro-F1. Model attribution on machine-translated text stays at \TrAllMin{}--\TrAllMax{}, and the five models, asked which model wrote each text, score \JudgeMin{}--\JudgeMax{}. Non-English machine text can therefore be attributed with a classifier whose decisions can be read, which matters for provenance checks that cannot rely on a fine-tuned black box.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
authorship attribution, AI-generated text, multilingual text mining, interpretable features, large language models
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Most work on machine-generated text asks whether a text was written by a person or by a model. A second question matters for provenance: \emph{which} model wrote it. We ask two things: can five frontier models be told apart from a small set of readable features in seven languages, and what does that readability cost against character $n$-grams? The model-attribution literature is mostly English~\cite{uchendu2020authorship,sun2025idiosyncrasies}, and the two multilingual studies we know of use fine-tuned or probability-based classifiers whose decisions cannot be read~\cite{lacava2026multilingual,greco2026multighost}.

The answer matters to people who cannot act on a probability from a model they cannot inspect. A platform moderator tracing a coordinated campaign in Hindi, or a teacher asked which model wrote a Turkish essay, needs a reason that can be stated: this text has the paragraphing and punctuation habits of one model and not another. A black-box score gives no such reason, and a fine-tuned detector for each language and model version rarely exists outside English.

There are two reasons to doubt that English results carry over. Models see far less training text in lower-resource languages~\cite{joshi2020state}, so their writing there may be less distinctive, and languages differ in script and morphology, so many stylometric measures are undefined outside English while those that are defined may track the language more than the author. Character $n$-grams, the single most successful feature in authorship attribution~\cite{sapkota2015ngrams}, have the opposite problem: they see vocabulary and morphology, so they are tied to the script and lexicon they were fit on.

We address both problems with a design that holds content fixed across languages and describes every text with features computed the same way on Universal Dependencies (UD) parses~\cite{nivre2020ud}, and we measure its cost against an $n$-gram baseline. Six questions were written down before data collection: whether five frontier models can be told apart within each of seven languages (\textbf{RQ1}), whether model attribution weakens as a language's resource level falls (\textbf{RQ2}), whether a model's style is shared across languages or specific to each (\textbf{RQ3}), whether the models converge on one style in lower-resource languages (\textbf{RQ4}), whether machine translation erases the signal (\textbf{RQ5}) and, as a baseline, whether the models themselves can identify the author (\textbf{RQ6}). The $n$-gram baseline and a feature-economy analysis were added afterwards.

We collect \NCollected{} content-matched essays (5 models $\times$ 7 languages $\times$ \NPrompts{} prompts $\times$ 2 generations) and \NTranslations{} machine translations, describe every text with \NFeatures{} features defined the same way in every language, and find that the features attribute the author in all seven languages at a modest, measured cost against $n$-grams; most of the signal sits in a handful of nameable features that survive machine translation, and the models themselves cannot do the task. Two pre-registered questions (resource gradient, convergence) return nulls.

\section{Related Work}
\textbf{Detection and stylometry.} Human-versus-machine detectors fine-tuned on English lose about a quarter of their F1 on other languages~\cite{macko2023multitude}. For human authors, character $n$-grams are the most successful single feature~\cite{sapkota2015ngrams}, masking all but the most frequent words isolates a structural signal~\cite{stamatatos2017distortion}, and UD-derived syntactic features attribute authors in several languages~\cite{gorman2022ud}.

\textbf{Model attribution.} In English, Uchendu et al.\ framed authorship attribution among neural generators~\cite{uchendu2020authorship}, Kumarage and Liu applied stylometric features to LLMs~\cite{kumarage2023neural}, Sun et al.\ showed that embedding classifiers separate model families and largely survive LLM translation into Chinese~\cite{sun2025idiosyncrasies}, and models optimized to fool detectors keep a distinct style~\cite{riverasoto2026attacks}. La Cava et al.\ attribute among seven older LLMs and human text in 18 languages with fine-tuned and probability-based detectors and find generators harder to distinguish in English~\cite{lacava2026multilingual}; MultiGhostBench attributes long-form text to five recent LLMs in six languages and finds fine-tuned transformers more language-independent than statistical detectors~\cite{greco2026multighost}. In Japanese, Zaitsu et al.\ attribute among six LLMs with part-of-speech and function-word features~\cite{zaitsu2026fingerprint}. To our knowledge, no prior which-model study uses one feature set with the same computational definition in every language, holds content fixed across languages, and compares that representation with character $n$-grams under matched adaptation within and across languages.

\textbf{Homogenization and LLM judges.} Writing with LLMs reduces the diversity of human text~\cite{padmakumar2024diversity}; whether models converge on each other as training data thins has not been tested. LLM evaluators favour their own outputs~\cite{panickssery2024self}, and models asked to name the author of a single English text score near chance and default to GPT or Claude~\cite{bai2025selfrecognition}; RQ6 repeats that task in seven languages, and a companion study examines self-recognition in English~\cite{erlikhman2026compllm}.

\section{Data and Method}
\subsection{Models, languages and prompts}
The five subject models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.7, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4 Pro) were queried through OpenRouter in September 2026, with the served model identifier logged for every response. The seven languages are English, Spanish, Chinese, Russian, Japanese, Turkish and Hindi, assigned ordinal resource ranks 1--7 in that order before data collection as a coarse proxy for their share of web training data. The ranking is contestable: Joshi et al.~\cite{joshi2020state} place English, Spanish, Chinese and Japanese in their highest class (5) and Russian, Turkish and Hindi one lower (4), so we report that two-class split beside the pre-registered order.

Twelve English prompt schemas each fix a topic, a stance (six for, six against), three supporting claims, a prose-only instruction and a reading-level tier. For each language a model that is not a subject (Llama 4 Maverick) wrote a native prompt from the schema rather than translating the English, so the wording is idiomatic while the content is fixed. A model from a third family (Qwen 3.7 Plus) read each of the 84 prompts blind, extracted topic, stance and claims, and compared them with the schema; failed prompts were regenerated with the reviewer's note until all 84 passed.

\subsection{Generation, validation and features}
Each prompt was sent as a single user turn with no system prompt at temperature 0.7, twice per cell with fixed seeds and hidden reasoning excluded from the output, giving $5 \times \NPrompts{} \times 7 \times 2 = \NCollected{}$ responses. Each passed language identification (confidence $\geq 0.6$), a 150--900 word-equivalent window and a per-language refusal check. One Grok response to a Hindi prompt was written in English and excluded, leaving \NResponses{} texts; ten DeepSeek responses that exhausted their token budget on hidden reasoning were re-collected with a larger budget.

Every text was parsed with Stanza~\cite{qi2020stanza}, with Chinese and Japanese pre-split on sentence-final punctuation. We compute \NFeatures{} features in five groups. \emph{Lexical}: moving-average type--token ratio (MATTR, window 50), hapax rate, mean token length, Zipf slope. \emph{Syntactic}: mean and SD of sentence length, burstiness of sentence length, mean maximum dependency depth, subordinate-clause rate (\texttt{acl}, \texttt{advcl}, \texttt{ccomp}, \texttt{xcomp}, \texttt{csubj} per sentence), function-word ratio, first-person rate. \emph{Structure}: paragraph count and length, question rate, connective rate. \emph{Punctuation}: commas, colons, dashes and semicolons per 1,000 tokens, with full-width and script variants mapped to the same feature. \emph{Character}: character-bigram entropy and digit rate.

\subsection{Analysis}
The two generations of a prompt are not independent, so every cross-validation split is leave-one-prompt-out (LOPO, \NPrompts{} folds), and accuracy intervals and GLM standard errors are prompt-clustered, while binomial, exact McNemar and judge tests treat texts as independent. The 28 headline comparisons (features and $n$-grams vs.\ chance, features vs.\ $n$-grams, features vs.\ the best judge, in seven languages) are Holm-corrected as one family; Spearman $p$-values over seven languages are exact permutation values. The pre-registered plan is \texttt{docs/analysis\_plan.md} in the repository.

\textbf{RQ1.} Within each language, multinomial logistic regression on standardized features. \textbf{Baseline.} TF-IDF over character 1--4-grams fit inside each training fold, then logistic regression; word 1--2-grams likewise. \textbf{RQ2.} A binomial GLM of cell-level correctness on resource rank with clustered standard errors (by prompt, by language, and by both), also with features residualized on log length within each language. \textbf{RQ3.} For each feature, a two-way ANOVA (model $\times$ language, prompt as a blocking factor) with partial $\eta^2$; and a transfer matrix in which features are z-scored within each language and a classifier trained on language $A$ is tested on $B$. For $n$-grams the counterpart fits the vocabulary on the union of $A$ and $B$ without labels and z-scores TF-IDF columns within each language, so both representations receive the same unlabelled adaptation. \textbf{RQ4.} After z-scoring within each language, the mean pairwise distance between the five model centroids, the silhouette of model labels and the between/within scatter ratio, with stratified bootstrap intervals. \textbf{RQ5.} All 120 English responses were translated into the six other languages by Google Translate and by an open non-subject model (MiniMax M3); we measure attribution on the translations alone, transfer from classifiers trained on the English originals or on native target-language responses (features z-scored within each set), and per-feature Spearman correlations between originals and translations. \textbf{RQ6.} Each subject model was asked, one text at a time with a shuffled candidate list and no metadata, which of the five wrote it (temperature 0, hidden reasoning off where the API allows), the exact-model-prediction task of Bai et al.~\cite{bai2025selfrecognition}. \textbf{Feature economy.} A nested feature-selection curve (within each LOPO fold, features are ranked by mean absolute standardized coefficient on the training fold only and the top $k$ are refit, for $k = 1, \dots, \NFeatures{}$); a per-language ablation of each feature group; and a character model that sees only punctuation, digits and whitespace, every word replaced by a placeholder~\cite{stamatatos2017distortion}, scored LOPO within language.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Model attribution works in every language, at a price}
Table~\ref{tab:main} shows five-way accuracy of \LRmin{}--\LRmax{} in every language; every prompt-clustered interval excludes chance and every Holm-corrected binomial has $p < 10^{-4}$. In plain terms, \NFeatures{} inspectable numbers identify the author about three times as often as guessing. Length is part of the signal: with features residualized on log length, logistic regression falls to \LRlenMin{}--\LRlenMax{}, still far above chance. Dropping the whole structure group costs at most \AblNoStructureWorst{} macro-F1 (Sec.~\ref{sec:economy}), so the signal is not paragraph count alone.

\textbf{The baseline is more accurate within a language.} Character $n$-grams reach \NGmin{}--\NGmax{}, \GapNGmin{}--\GapNGmax{} points above the features (mean \GapNGmean{}). Per-language McNemar tests on about 120 paired predictions are underpowered for gaps near ten points (Spanish: \GapNGes{} points, Holm \GapNGesHolmP{}); the advantage is Holm-significant in \NGsigLangs{} and in the same direction elsewhere. This is the expected result~\cite{sapkota2015ngrams}: $n$-grams see vocabulary and morphology, and the features do not; a practitioner with labelled data in the target language should prefer $n$-grams, and pay the gap only when the decision must be explained or must transfer.

\textbf{LLM judges (RQ6).} Asked one text at a time which of the five models wrote it, the judges score \Judgedeepseek{} (DeepSeek) to \Judgeclaude{} (Claude). Only Claude is above chance (\JudgeclaudeP{}), and only Claude names its own text more often than others' (own-text recall \JudgeclaudeOwn{} against \JudgeclaudeFalse{} false self-claims; Fisher \JudgeclaudeFisherP{}), the registered prediction; GPT-5.5 names itself for \JudgegptSelfClaim{} of texts regardless of author. The feature classifier exceeds the best judge by \GapJudgeMin{}--\GapJudgeMax{} points in every language (Holm $p < 10^{-4}$). Bai et al.~\cite{bai2025selfrecognition} report the same near-chance, GPT- and Claude-biased behaviour in English; it holds in all seven languages here, and a side-by-side lineup with reasoning enabled raises the same judges~\cite{erlikhman2026compllm}.

\subsection{What carries the signal}
\label{sec:economy}
By mean absolute standardized coefficient the strongest features are \TopCoefFeatures{}. In the two-way ANOVA, language explains far more feature variance than model (mean partial $\eta^2$ \EtaLang{} against \EtaModel{}; interaction \EtaInter{}; prompt \EtaPrompt{}), while model effects are largest for \EtaModelTopFive{} and smallest for subordination, question rate and dependency depth ($\leq \EtaModelSmallMax{}$): the models differ in lexical variety, punctuation and paragraphing, hardly at all in clause structure.

The nested selection curve (Fig.~\ref{fig:feat}a) ranks features on the training folds only. In each language the five highest-ranked features reach \CurveKfiveShareMin{}--\CurveKfiveShareMax{}\% of the full set's macro-F1 (\CurveKfiveMin{}--\CurveKfiveMax{} against \CurveKtwentyoneMin{}--\CurveKtwentyoneMax{}), but the smallest number of features within 0.03 of a language's best score ranges from \CurveKneeMin{} (\CurveKneeMinLang{}) to \CurveKneeMax{} (\CurveKneeMaxLang{}), and the ranking changes with language: paragraph count is \ParaCountRankRu{} in Russian and \ParaCountRankEn{} in English. The pooled order is \PooledTopFive{}. No single group is required: dropping any one costs at most \AblMaxDrop{} macro-F1 (\AblMaxDropWhere{}); structure alone gives \AblStructMin{}--\AblStructMax{} and punctuation alone \AblPunctMin{}--\AblPunctMax{}. The punctuation, digit and whitespace model attributes at \PunctDiagMin{}--\PunctDiagMax{} within language, so segmentation, punctuation and length alone carry a signal.

\subsection{Across languages and through translation}
\label{sec:transfer}
\textbf{Cross-language transfer (RQ3).} After within-language z-scoring (Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}a), a classifier trained on any language reaches \TransferMin{}--\TransferMax{} on any other (mean \TransferOff{}, against \TransferDiag{} within language), all 42 off-diagonal cells exceed chance after Holm correction, and \TransferChanceCorrected{} of the above-chance accuracy transfers. Given the same unlabelled adaptation, character $n$-grams transfer at mean \NGFairOff{} (Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}b), above chance in \NGFairAbove{} of 42 cells; the features are better in \FeatBeatsNGCells{} of the 42 cells, and $n$-grams keep their edge where script and vocabulary are shared. Without adaptation, $n$-grams transfer at \NGTransferOff{}. Two caveats: the test language contains the \NPrompts{} training prompts, so off-diagonal cells are an upper bound for unseen prompts, and both representations use the test language's unlabelled statistics.

\caption{Cross-language transfer: a classifier trained on one language (rows) is tested on another (columns) after within-language z-scoring; the diagonal is LOPO within language. (a) UD features. (b) Character $n$-grams given the same adaptation (union vocabulary, TF-IDF columns z-scored per language).}
\label{fig:transfer}

\textbf{Translation (RQ5).} Classifiers trained and tested on the translations alone (LOPO) reach \TrAllMin{}--\TrAllMax{}, every interval excluding chance, about \TrCostPts{} points below the English originals (\LRen{}) and close to native responses in the six languages (mean \TrNativeMean{}); $n$-grams retrained on the translations reach \NGTrLopoMin{}--\NGTrLopoMax{}. Which features pass through (Fig.~\ref{fig:feat}b): paragraph count ($\rho = \Survparacount{}$), paragraph length (\Survparalenmean{}), digit rate (\Survdigitrate{}) and sentence length (\Survsentlenmean{}) are preserved largely by construction, since both translators keep paragraph and sentence boundaries and copy digits; hapax rate (\Survhapaxrate{}), Zipf slope (\Survzipfslope{}) and comma rate (\Survcommaperk{}) survive with some loss; MATTR (\Survmattr{}), function-word ratio (\Survfuncwordratio{}) and bigram entropy (\Survbigramentropy{}) are rewritten by the target language. A classifier trained on the English originals is correct on \TrTrainEnMean{} of their translations with either translator; because it has seen every source text, this is a same-text stability measure rather than accuracy on new texts. A classifier trained on native responses in the target language, which has seen none of these texts, reads them at \TrGoogleTrainNative{}--\TrLLMTrainNative{}. An English-trained $n$-gram model with no vocabulary adaptation scores \NGTrTrainEnNonEsMin{}--\NGTrTrainEnNonEsMax{} on every target language except Spanish (\NGTrTrainEnEs{}), including Latin-script Turkish, so the loss is vocabulary rather than script.

\subsection{Two pre-registered questions with null answers}
\textbf{Resource gradient (RQ2).} The cell-level GLM gives $\beta = \Beta{}$ log-odds per rank step (SE \BetaSE{}, 95\% CI \BetaLo{} to \BetaHi{}, \BetaP{} clustered by prompt; \BetaLangP{} by language, a standard error resting on seven clusters; \BetaLangPromptP{} by both). The point estimate is under one accuracy point per step, and the ordering is not monotone (Japanese matches English; Hindi exceeds Spanish and Turkish), all within intervals of about $\pm$\ClusterCIhalfwidth{} points. The minimum detectable effect at 80\% power is about \MDEpts{} points over the six steps and the interval admits a decline of up to \SteepestDeclinePts{}, so this is a null with bounded power rather than a demonstration of invariance. Joshi's two classes give the same picture (mean \ClassFiveMean{} for the four Class-5 languages against \ClassFourMean{} for the three Class-4 ones), as does the $n$-gram baseline (Hindi \NGhi{} exceeds English \NGen{}; GLM \NGglmP{}).

\textbf{Convergence (RQ4).} Mean distance between model centroids falls from \CentEn{} $z$-units in English to \CentHi{} in Hindi (Spearman $\rho = \CentRho{}$ against rank, \CentPexact{}) and the between/within scatter ratio from \BWen{} to \BWhi{} ($\rho = \BWrho{}$, \BWPexact{}), with the Hindi intervals below the English ones; but the silhouette is \SilMin{} to \SilMax{} in every language, its English and Hindi intervals overlap ([\SilEnLo{}, \SilEnHi{}] against [\SilHiLo{}, \SilHiHi{}]), and the pre-registered rule (all three intervals separated) is not met. The change is located in one model: the mean of the four pairwise distances involving Grok falls from \GrokPairsEn{} in English to \GrokPairsHi{} in Hindi, while the mean of the six other pairs is \OtherPairsEn{} in English and \OtherPairsHi{} in Hindi ($\rho = \OtherPairsRho{}$, \OtherPairsPexact{}). Grok's English register is the outlier that disappears outside English; the other four models are as far apart in Hindi as in English. La Cava et al.\ find generators harder to separate in English~\cite{lacava2026multilingual}; neither their result nor ours supports a general convergence claim.

\section{Discussion}
Interpretable authorship attribution does not require English: the three Class-4 languages average \ClassFourMean{} against \ClassFiveMean{} for the four Class-5 languages, inside the $\pm$\ClusterCIhalfwidth{}-point intervals, and a classifier trained in one language transfers to the others after unlabelled standardization. The choice of representation depends on where the classifier will be used: within one language, with labelled data, character $n$-grams are the better tool by \GapNGmin{}--\GapNGmax{} points; across scripts under equal adaptation the features transfer better, and where script and vocabulary are shared, $n$-grams keep their edge. For this genre and model snapshot, machine translation does not remove the signal, and the surviving features can be named; translation combined with a paraphrase attack~\cite{riverasoto2026attacks} is untested.

\textbf{Dual use.} Nothing in the features is specific to machine-generated text, and human attribution already uses UD-derived features~\cite{gorman2022ud}, so the release makes public a method rather than a new capability; the translation result is a caution for pseudonymous writers. We release model-generated text only.

\textbf{Limitations.} (i) One genre, persuasive essays with three fixed claims and no lists, so paragraph count and length partly record how each model lays out an argument; both translators keep paragraph boundaries. (ii) Length is entangled with style; the transfer, convergence and translation analyses are not length-controlled. (iii) The resource ranking is coarse, and the RQ2 interval admits a \SteepestDeclinePts{}-point decline. (iv) Eight of the \NFeatures{} features depend on Stanza parses or sentence splitting; parser accuracy varies by language without following the resource order (Hindi and Russian parse best, Turkish and Chinese worst~\cite{qi2020stanza}), and four of the five top pooled features are parser-free. (v) The transfer and translation tests share the same \NPrompts{} prompts across languages, two generations per cell give intervals of about $\pm$\ClusterCIhalfwidth{} points, and prompt fidelity was checked by a model, not by native speakers. (vi) All five subjects are closed APIs served in September 2026; open-weight models, adversarial rewriting and a fine-tuned multilingual encoder baseline~\cite{greco2026multighost} were not tested, and judges ran without extended reasoning.

\section{Conclusion}
Across seven languages, \NFeatures{} interpretable features with one definition in every language attribute persuasive essays to one of five frontier LLMs at \LRmin{}--\LRmax{} accuracy, \GapNGmin{}--\GapNGmax{} points below character $n$-grams within a language and \TransferOff{} against \NGFairOff{} across languages under the same unlabelled adaptation. Most of the signal sits in a handful of nameable features, led in the pooled ranking by paragraph count and length, which pass through machine translation almost unchanged, so non-English machine text can be attributed with a classifier whose decisions can be read. Future work: other genres, human-verified prompts, adapted $n$-grams on translations and a multilingual encoder baseline.
